# Tint a photo

- Route: `/tools/tint-photo`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `tint-photo`

## Summary

Lay a color over a photo like a filter on a lens: pick warming, cooling, sepia or any custom color, set the density, and keep the brightness where it was. (Photo editing)

## Details

This page opens Aperture, the Media Manipulator photo editor, with the Photo filter panel in front and the Warming filter loaded at Density 25 with Preserve luminosity on. A photo filter here does what a glass filter does on a lens: each pixel is multiplied by the filter color, and the Density slider decides how far from the original toward that filtered value the pixel moves. With Preserve luminosity the result is then scaled back so its BT.709 luma equals the original, which gives a tint without a darkening. Six filter chips, Warming, Cooling, Sepia, Red, Green and Blue, set the color, and Custom color takes any hex value. For a sepia print, stack it on a Black & white layer.
### What it does
- Loads a Photo filter layer with the Warming color #ec8a00 at Density 25 on open, and gives you Cooling #0a5dc8, Sepia #ac7a33, Red #e81c1c, Green #1fb52f, Blue #1c3ee8 and a Custom color picker.
- Density runs from 0 to 100: at 0 the layer does nothing, at 100 every pixel is fully multiplied by the filter color, and between the two it is a straight blend.
- Preserve luminosity, on by default, rescales each tinted pixel so its luma matches the untinted pixel, which keeps the exposure of the photo and turns the filter into a pure color shift.
- Works as a layer like everything else: mask it to tint only the sky, lower its opacity, set the blend mode to Color so it never touches luminance at all, and undo at any time.
- Exports the tinted photo at full resolution from the original pixels as JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF.
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: The editor opens on the Photo filter panel with Warming at 25 percent density already applied as a layer.
2. Pick the color: Choose Warming, Cooling, Sepia, Red, Green or Blue, or enter a custom hex color for a brand tint.
3. Set the density: Drag Density until the tint is as strong as you want, and switch Preserve luminosity off only if you want the filter to darken as a real glass filter would.
4. Export: Choose the format and quality; the server renders the tint on the original and names the file (retouched).
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- A photo filter is three multiplies and a blend per pixel; a 45 megapixel export is rendered in a few seconds and the time goes to encoding.
- TIFF output keeps 8 bits per channel; the tint is applied before encoding, so the TIFF is the rendered result, not the original plus a layer.
### Technical details
- The formula per channel is lerp(c, c x f, Density / 100), where c is the pixel in sRGB 0..1 and f is the filter color in the same scale; Warming #ec8a00 is f = (0.9255, 0.5412, 0). Because the filter multiplies, it can only lower a channel, and a channel whose filter value is 0, blue under Warming, is scaled by exactly 1 - Density / 100.
- With Preserve luminosity the editor computes the BT.709 luma of the original, L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, and of the tinted pixel, and multiplies the tinted pixel by their ratio, then clamps to 0..1. A mid gray of 0.5 under Warming at Density 25 becomes (0.4907, 0.4427, 0.375) before the rescale, which has luma 0.448; the ratio 1.116 lifts it to (0.5477, 0.4941, 0.4185), levels (140, 126, 107).
- Clamping limits preservation near white: a pure white under Warming at 25 percent would need red above 1 to keep its luma, so it clamps and exports as (255, 252, 213), slightly darker than the source. Highlights therefore lose a little brightness at high densities even with the option on.
- A filter at 100 percent density with Preserve luminosity is a pure chromatic shift toward the filter color, not a flat fill: the pixel keeps its original luma, so a sepia at 100 on a mid gray gives (172, 122, 51), still a mid-tone.
- The preview you adjust is drawn by WebGL2 on your GPU from a 1920 px copy of the photo; the download is rendered on our server from the original with the same multiply, blend and luma rescale, within the documented tolerance for color stages of a mean error of at most 1 and a maximum of 4 levels out of 255.
### When not to use it
A photo filter adds a cast; it is not the tool for removing one, because multiplying by a color cannot restore a channel that the light took away, and the white balance page does that in linear light with a temperature and tint pair. When you want the shadows one color and the highlights another, split toning has a slider for each end plus a balance between them. For a complete grade from a reference file, a .cube LUT in the LUT panel reproduces it in one layer. A tint on a photo that is also underexposed should wait until exposure is fixed, since the luma rescale preserves whatever brightness is there.
### Use cases
- Warm a cold frame: Overcast and shade push photos blue; Warming at 20 to 35 percent brings back the color of sun without changing exposure.
- Sepia prints: A Black & white layer followed by Sepia at 50 to 70 percent with Preserve luminosity on gives the classic brown print.
- Brand color wash: Enter the brand hex as the custom color and keep Density low so product shots across a page share one cast.
- Cool a night scene: Cooling at 30 to 40 percent pushes a street at night toward blue while the sodium lamps keep their relative warmth.
### FAQ
Q: What is the difference between a tint and a white balance change?
A: White balance works in linear light and shifts the midtones along the blue-yellow and green-magenta axes to correct the light the photo was shot in. A photo filter multiplies by any color in gamma space with a density, which is a creative wash rather than a correction. Use white balance to fix a cast and a filter to add one.
Q: Why does the photo get darker when I turn off Preserve luminosity?
A: The filter multiplies each channel by the filter color, and every filter value is at most 1, so without the rescale the tinted pixel can only be as bright or darker. Warming has a blue value of 0, so at full density the blue channel is removed entirely.
Q: How do I make a sepia photo?
A: Add a Black & white layer first, then a Photo filter with the Sepia chip at a density of 50 to 70 percent and Preserve luminosity on. A mid gray of 128 at 50 percent becomes (142, 126, 102); at 100 percent it becomes (172, 122, 51).
Q: Can I tint only the sky or only the shadows?
A: Yes. Give the Photo filter layer a mask: a Linear gradient from the top for a sky, or a Luminosity range from 0 to about 0.3 for the shadows. The tint is then blended by the mask value per pixel.
Q: What hex color should I use for a vintage look?
A: The Sepia chip is #ac7a33. Warmer and lighter, #d9a66b at 30 to 40 percent reads as a faded print; a cold vintage is Cooling #0a5dc8 at 15 percent over a Fade look from the Looks panel.
Q: Does the tint change a transparent PNG?
A: Only the color channels. Alpha is never touched by any adjustment, so a product cutout keeps its transparent background and the tint shows only on the visible pixels.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when someone wants to lay a colour over a photo like a lens filter: warming, cooling, sepia, red, green, blue or a custom colour, at a chosen density while keeping brightness. Typical asks: "give this photo a warm tone".
When to send them elsewhere: To remove a cast rather than add one use White balance (white-balance-photo). For different colours in shadows and highlights use Split toning (split-toning). To apply an existing .cube grade use Apply a LUT (apply-lut-to-photo).
